title: The Cambrian Period and Paleozoic Era begin
summary: The Paleozoic opens; its base is fixed at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, by the first complex burrows of the trace fossil Treptichnus pedum.
description: The base of the Cambrian Period, and with it the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon, is defined by a boundary stratotype at Fortune Head on Newfoundland's Burin Peninsula. The marker is the first appearance of Treptichnus pedum, a branching burrow made by a mobile, worm-like animal probing the sediment, which signals more complex behaviour than is seen in the Ediacaran. The boundary is dated to about 538.8 million years ago using volcanic ash beds elsewhere, notably in Namibia. The choice of marker has been criticised because T. pedum was later found somewhat below the boundary at the type section, and some geologists have proposed redefining it.

title: Cambrian explosion
summary: Within roughly 20 million years most major animal phyla appear in the fossil record, along with shells, eyes, legs and active predators.
description: The Cambrian explosion is the geologically rapid appearance, over roughly 20–25 million years, of most of the animal body plans (phyla) alive today, including arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, echinoderms and chordates. Mineralised skeletons, compound eyes, deep burrowing and active predation spread through the oceans, and exceptional deposits such as Chengjiang and the Burgess Shale preserve soft-bodied forms. Proposed drivers include rising oxygen in the oceans, changes in seawater chemistry that favoured skeleton-building, the evolution of developmental gene networks, and ecological arms races between predators and prey. How 'explosive' it was is still debated: Ediacaran animals and trace fossils show earlier roots, and molecular clocks place the divergence of many animal lineages tens of millions of years before the Cambrian.

title: Flood geology: the strata as Noah's Flood
dateLabel: Claimed: a single year a few thousand years ago (applied to rocks 538.8–251.9 million years old)
summary: Young-Earth creationists claim that the Paleozoic rocks and their fossils were laid down in a single year by Noah's Flood, a few thousand years ago.
description: Flood geology, set out by the Seventh-day Adventist writer George McCready Price in The New Geology (1923) and revived by John Whitcomb and Henry Morris in The Genesis Flood (1961), holds that most of the fossil-bearing rock record was deposited during a single, year-long global flood described in the Book of Genesis. Many flood geologists place the onset of the Flood at the Great Unconformity beneath the Cambrian strata, conspicuously exposed in the Grand Canyon, and read the Paleozoic succession of marine fossils as sea-floor communities buried early in the Flood. They explain the consistent order of fossils by ecological zonation, hydrodynamic sorting of carcasses and the ability of more mobile animals to flee rising water, and some invoke 'catastrophic plate tectonics' to move the continents within the Flood year. The idea remains central to young-Earth creationist organisations such as Answers in Genesis and the Institute for Creation Research.
mainstreamView: Geologists, many of them clergymen, abandoned the idea that a single flood laid down the strata in the early 19th century, and the evidence against it has since grown overwhelming. Radiometric dates from volcanic ash beds within the Paleozoic succession span almost 300 million years, and the rocks contain features that cannot form in one flood: fossil soils, reefs built up in place over long periods, wind-blown dune sandstones such as the Permian Coconino Sandstone of the Grand Canyon, thick evaporites, repeated glacial deposits, and burrows and trackways at many levels. The fossil order does not match sorting by density, habitat or mobility; microfossils of similar size and shape still appear in a consistent sequence worldwide, and no flowering plants, mammals or birds occur among Paleozoic fossils. Flood geology is therefore regarded as pseudoscience by the scientific community.

title: Intelligent design and the Cambrian explosion
dateLabel: c. 530 million years ago (as proponents frame it)
summary: Intelligent-design advocates argue that the Cambrian explosion was too abrupt for evolution and points to a designing intelligence.
description: Proponents of intelligent design, most prominently Stephen C. Meyer in his book Darwin's Doubt (2013), argue that the geologically sudden appearance of many animal body plans in the early Cambrian cannot be explained by mutation and natural selection. They contend that building new body plans required large amounts of new genetic information in too short a time, and that the lack of clear Precambrian ancestors for most phyla points to design rather than descent with modification. The argument draws on a genuine puzzle that Charles Darwin himself acknowledged in On the Origin of Species, where he called the abrupt appearance of Cambrian fossils a serious difficulty for his theory.
mainstreamView: Palaeontologists and evolutionary biologists reject the design inference. The 'explosion' unfolded over roughly 20–25 million years and was preceded by Ediacaran animals, increasingly complex trace fossils and small shelly fossils, so it was not instantaneous. Developmental genetics and molecular clocks show that the genetic toolkit for building animal bodies predates the Cambrian, and stem-group fossils such as lobopodians and early arthropods document intermediate stages. Reviewers including palaeontologist Charles Marshall criticised Darwin's Doubt for misrepresenting this evidence, and intelligent design is not regarded as a testable scientific theory; a US federal court (Kitzmiller v. Dover, 2005) ruled that it is a form of creationism.

title: First trilobites
summary: Trilobites appear in Siberia and Morocco and become the iconic armoured arthropods of Paleozoic seas for the next 270 million years.
description: The oldest trilobite body fossils, such as Profallotaspis in Siberia and Fallotaspis in Morocco's Anti-Atlas, appear around 521 million years ago, in the second series of the Cambrian. Their calcite-reinforced exoskeletons fossilised readily, and their rapid evolution makes them the main tool for subdividing Cambrian and Ordovician rocks. Trilobites had compound eyes with lenses made of calcite, among the earliest sophisticated visual systems known. Earlier trace fossils such as Rusophycus, attributed to trilobite-like arthropods, suggest their lineage is somewhat older than the first skeletons. Trilobites declined after the Late Devonian extinctions and the last of them died out in the end-Permian extinction.

title: Chengjiang biota
summary: Fine mudstones near Chengjiang, Yunnan, preserve soft-bodied Cambrian animals in remarkable detail, including guts, nerves and eyes.
description: The Chengjiang biota of the Maotianshan Shale in Yunnan, China, was discovered by Hou Xianguang in 1984 and is about ten million years older than Canada's Burgess Shale. More than 250 species have been described, among them early arthropods, lobopodians, priapulid worms, sponges and some of the earliest known chordates and vertebrates. Rapid burial in fine sediment preserved soft tissues such as digestive tracts and, in some arthropods, traces of the nervous system. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, it provides one of the earliest detailed snapshots of the Cambrian explosion.

title: First vertebrates: Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia
summary: Fish-like animals about 2.5–3 cm long from the Chengjiang biota, with a head, eyes and gill pouches, are among the oldest known vertebrates.
description: Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys, described from the Chengjiang biota in 1999, were small jawless animals about 2.5–3 centimetres long with a distinct head, paired eyes, gill pouches, zigzag muscle blocks and a dorsal fin. Many palaeontologists regard them as the earliest known vertebrates or close stem-vertebrates, placing the origin of the lineage that includes all fishes and, eventually, humans in the early Cambrian. They lacked bone; mineralised skeletons appear in vertebrates only later, in the armoured jawless fishes of the Ordovician. Metaspriggina from the Burgess Shale and Marble Canyon in Canada shows a similar body plan roughly 10–13 million years later.

title: Emu Bay Shale
summary: On Kangaroo Island, South Australia, the Emu Bay Shale preserves the eyes of the predator Anomalocaris, each with over 16,000 lenses.
description: The Emu Bay Shale on the north coast of Kangaroo Island is an early Cambrian fossil deposit with exceptional soft-tissue preservation. It has yielded trilobites such as Redlichia, the bivalved arthropod Isoxys and, in 2011, isolated compound eyes of the apex predator Anomalocaris, each bearing more than 16,000 lenses. These eyes showed that some Cambrian predators had visual acuity rivalling that of many modern insects and crustaceans. The deposit is Australia's most important window on the Cambrian explosion.

title: Early Cambrian extinctions and Kalkarindji eruptions
summary: A series of early Cambrian extinctions, partly coinciding with vast basalt eruptions in northern Australia, devastates archaeocyathan reefs.
description: Late in the early Cambrian, a series of extinctions often grouped as the end-Botomian crisis devastated the archaeocyathan sponges that built the first animal reefs, along with many trilobites and small shelly fossils. An early pulse, the Sinsk event, is linked to oxygen-poor water spreading across the Siberian Platform. A later pulse near the transition to the middle Cambrian coincides closely with the Kalkarindji large igneous province, which covered more than two million square kilometres of northern Australia with basalt around 511 million years ago and is the oldest known Phanerozoic large igneous province. Volcanic gases may have driven warming and ocean anoxia, a pattern repeated in later mass extinctions, although the scale of these Cambrian extinctions and their exact correlation with the eruptions remain under study.

title: Burgess Shale
summary: High in the Canadian Rockies, the Burgess Shale preserves a soft-bodied Cambrian community including Opabinia, Hallucigenia and Anomalocaris.
description: The Burgess Shale in Yoho National Park, British Columbia, was discovered by Charles Walcott in 1909 and records a marine community of about 508 million years ago buried by mud flows at the foot of a submarine reef escarpment. It preserves soft-bodied animals that rarely fossilise, such as the five-eyed Opabinia, the spiny lobopodian Hallucigenia, the large predator Anomalocaris and the early chordate Pikaia. Restudy of its fossils from the 1970s, popularised by Stephen Jay Gould's book Wonderful Life (1989), made it central to debates about the tempo and pattern of early animal evolution. Many of its once-puzzling 'weird wonders' are now placed in the stem groups of living phyla, especially the arthropods.

title: Meister Print: a 'shoe print' on trilobites
dateLabel: Rocks c. 505 million years old (find made in 1968)
summary: A shoe-shaped mark found in 1968 on a slab of Cambrian shale in Utah, with trilobites beneath its "heel", is claimed as a human footprint.
description: In 1968 the amateur collector William Meister, splitting slabs of the Cambrian Wheeler Shale near Antelope Spring in Utah's House Range in search of trilobites, opened one to reveal a shape resembling the print of a sandal or shoe, with small trilobites of the species Elrathia kingii apparently crushed beneath it. The Wheeler Shale is about 505 million years old, far older than any land vertebrate, let alone humans. Young-Earth creationists, beginning with the chemist Melvin Cook in 1970, promoted the slab as proof that humans and trilobites lived together, contradicting evolution and the geological timescale. It is still cited in some creationist and 'out-of-place artefact' literature.
mainstreamView: Geologists and palaeontologists who examined the slab concluded that the 'print' is a spall, a piece of rock that broke away along natural fractures to leave a shape that only vaguely resembles a shoe. It shows none of the features of a genuine footprint: there is only one isolated mark rather than a trackway, the surrounding mud shows no deformation or displacement, and the outline matches spalling patterns common in the Wheeler Shale. Trilobites are among the most abundant fossils in these beds, so their presence near the mark is unremarkable, and no human or other land-animal remains have ever been found in Cambrian rocks.

title: Late Cambrian extinctions and the SPICE event
summary: A worldwide carbon-isotope shift, the SPICE event, coincides with repeated extinctions of shallow-water trilobites in the late Cambrian.
description: The Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion (SPICE), first described in 1993 from Cambrian rocks of the Great Basin of Nevada and Utah and since traced on several continents, is a marked rise in the proportion of carbon-13 in marine carbonates between about 497 and 494 million years ago. It coincides with the 'biomere' extinctions, a pattern recognised by the palaeontologist Allison Palmer in the 1960s, in which shallow-water trilobite faunas were repeatedly wiped out and replaced by trilobites migrating up from deeper, cooler water. The excursion is thought to reflect increased burial of organic carbon and pyrite as oxygen-poor and sulfidic water spread across continental shelves, accompanied by changes in sea level and cooling of shallow seas. Some researchers have proposed that this burial raised atmospheric oxygen and helped set the stage for the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, although the size and causes of the late Cambrian extinctions remain under study.

title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event
summary: Marine life diversifies dramatically, with the number of families roughly tripling as reefs and plankton-based ecosystems take shape.
description: Over roughly 25 million years of the Early and Middle Ordovician, marine biodiversity rose to several times its Cambrian level in the largest sustained radiation of the Paleozoic. Brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, corals, cephalopods, graptolites and plankton diversified, and new reef and filter-feeding communities formed that would dominate the seas until the end-Permian extinction. Suggested causes include global cooling towards a more temperate climate, rising oxygen, high sea levels flooding continental shelves, widely dispersed continents and increased nutrient supply; a meteorite shower around 466 million years ago has also been invoked. Because its timing differs between regions and groups, many researchers treat it as a set of overlapping radiations rather than a single event.

title: Fezouata biota
summary: Shales near Zagora, Morocco, preserve soft-bodied Early Ordovician animals, showing that Burgess-type creatures outlived the Cambrian.
description: The Fezouata Formation of Morocco's Anti-Atlas, reported as an exceptional fossil site in 2010, preserves soft-bodied animals from the Early Ordovician. It includes late-surviving Cambrian-style groups such as marrellomorph arthropods, lobopodians and giant filter-feeding radiodonts like the two-metre Aegirocassis, alongside early members of groups that radiated in the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event. The site showed that the scarcity of Burgess-type animals after the Cambrian partly reflects a lack of exceptional preservation rather than their extinction. Because it lay at high southern latitudes on the margin of Gondwana, it also offers a rare view of a cold-water Ordovician ecosystem.

title: First land plants
summary: Spores of the earliest known land plants, small liverwort-like embryophytes, appear in Ordovician rocks of Argentina as plants begin to green the land.
description: The oldest widely accepted evidence of land plants is cryptospores, tough-walled spores in distinctive tetrads and pairs, from rocks about 470 million years old in north-western Argentina, with similar spores soon appearing worldwide. The plants that produced them were small, probably resembling modern liverworts, and lacked water-conducting tissues; they likely relied on partnerships with fungi to extract nutrients from bare ground. Their spread began to transform weathering, soils and the carbon cycle, and some researchers link it to the cooling of the Late Ordovician. Molecular-clock studies place the origin of land plants earlier, around 500 million years ago or more in the Cambrian, so the fossil record may capture their rise to abundance rather than their very first appearance.

title: Ordovician meteor event
summary: A collision in the asteroid belt showers Earth with L-chondrite meteorites, leaving fossil meteorites in Swedish limestone.
description: In the Middle Ordovician, a large asteroid, the parent body of today's common L-chondrite meteorites, broke apart in the asteroid belt, and for perhaps a few million years Earth received a flux of meteorites and dust one to two orders of magnitude above normal. Fossil meteorites and meteoritic chromite grains preserved in limestone at Kinnekulle and other Swedish quarries record the shower, and several impact craters of similar age are known, including Lockne in Sweden. Some researchers have linked the extra extraterrestrial dust to global cooling and to phases of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, but these causal links remain debated. A 2024 study further proposed that Earth may briefly have had a ring of debris, an idea that has yet to be widely tested.

title: Sacabambaspis and the armoured jawless fishes
summary: In Bolivia, Sacabambaspis, a jawless fish with a bony head shield and forward-set eyes, records some of the first vertebrates with bone.
description: Sacabambaspis janvieri, described in 1986 from Middle Ordovician sandstones near Sacabamba in Bolivia's Cochabamba Department, is one of the most completely known early vertebrates. It was a jawless fish about 35 centimetres long including its slender tail, with a head shield of bony plates, small forward-placed eyes and a fixed, open mouth, probably feeding on small particles in shallow coastal waters on the margin of Gondwana. Together with Arandaspis from Australia and Astraspis from North America, it belongs to the Ordovician radiation of armoured jawless fishes, among the first vertebrates to have bony tissues. Its fossils often occur in mass-mortality beds, possibly caused by storms or influxes of fresh water.

title: Hirnantian glaciation
summary: A short, intense ice age centred on Gondwana, then over the South Pole, spreads ice sheets across what is now the Sahara.
description: During the latest Ordovician Hirnantian Stage, ice sheets built up over the supercontinent Gondwana, whose north-African region then lay near the South Pole. Glacial striations, tunnel valleys and tillites from this glaciation are preserved across the Sahara, notably in Algeria and Libya, and related deposits occur in South America and South Africa. Global sea level fell by an estimated 50–100 metres or more and tropical seas cooled sharply, triggering the first pulse of the end-Ordovician mass extinction. The glacial maximum lasted less than two million years, although glaciation in Gondwana had begun earlier in the Ordovician and recurred intermittently into the Silurian.

title: End-Ordovician mass extinction
summary: The first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions eliminates an estimated 85% of marine species in two pulses tied to glaciation.
description: The Late Ordovician mass extinction struck in two main pulses near the start and end of the Hirnantian glaciation and is estimated to have eliminated about 85% of marine species, making it the second-largest of the 'Big Five' by proportion of species lost. The first pulse coincided with cooling and the fall in sea level that drained shallow continental seas, hitting brachiopods, trilobites, graptolites and conodonts; the second accompanied deglaciation and the spread of oxygen-poor water. Because nearly all life was still marine and surviving groups rebounded in the Silurian, its long-term ecological effects were smaller than its taxonomic toll suggests. Proposed contributing factors include volcanism, changing ocean chemistry and toxic metals, while a suggestion that a nearby gamma-ray burst stripped away the ozone layer has attracted attention but lacks direct evidence. The recovery interval is recorded in graptolite-bearing shales at Dob's Linn in southern Scotland, where the base of the Silurian is formally defined.

title: Earliest jawed fishes
summary: Fossils from south China, including the tiny placoderm Xiushanosteus, are the oldest articulated jawed vertebrates yet found.
description: Jaws evolved from the skeletal arches that support the gills and allowed vertebrates to become efficient predators of larger prey; almost all living vertebrates, including humans, are jawed gnathostomes. Isolated scales and spines had long hinted at an Ordovician or early Silurian origin, but complete fossils were lacking until 2022, when researchers described articulated jawed fishes about 436 million years old from the Chongqing Lagerstätte, among them the placoderm Xiushanosteus and the shark-like Shenacanthus, together with spines and scales of the slightly older Fanjingshania from Guizhou. Younger Silurian fossils from Yunnan, such as the bony fish Guiyu and the placoderm Entelognathus with modern-looking jaw bones, show that jawed fishes diversified rapidly in the seas of the South China block.

title: Cooksonia, an early vascular plant
summary: Cooksonia, a few centimetres tall with forked stems tipped by spore capsules, is among the earliest known vascular land plants.
description: Cooksonia was a small, leafless plant with branching stems topped by spore-producing sporangia, first described from rocks of the Welsh Borderland and named after the Australian palaeobotanist Isabel Cookson. The oldest specimens, from Silurian rocks of County Tipperary in Ireland, are about 433 million years old, and the genus persisted into the Early Devonian. Some specimens preserve tracheids, the water-conducting cells that allowed vascular plants to stand upright and eventually grow tall. It is often treated as a model of the earliest vascular plants, although fossils assigned to Cooksonia may belong to several different lineages.

title: Caledonian orogeny closes the Iapetus Ocean
summary: Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collide, closing the Iapetus Ocean and raising mountains from Appalachia through Scotland to Norway.
description: The Caledonian orogeny was a series of mountain-building episodes as the Iapetus Ocean narrowed and closed between the continents of Laurentia, Baltica and the microcontinent Avalonia. Its climax, the Scandian phase around 430–400 million years ago, joined Scotland (part of Laurentia) to England (part of Avalonia) and drove Baltica beneath Greenland, forming a Himalaya-scale range whose roots survive in the Scottish Highlands, Scandinavia and East Greenland. The collisions created the continent Laurussia, also called Euramerica or the Old Red Sandstone continent after the red river sediments shed from the eroding mountains. The Iapetus suture runs today beneath northern England and central Ireland, which is why earlier fossils on either side of it differ, an observation that helped J. Tuzo Wilson propose in 1966 that oceans can close and reopen.

title: Earliest known land animals: Scottish millipedes
summary: Millipedes from Scotland, such as Kampecaris and the air-breathing Pneumodesmus, are among the oldest known fully land-living animals.
description: Fossil millipedes from Scotland are among the oldest body fossils of animals that lived fully on land: Pneumodesmus newmani from Cowie Harbour near Stonehaven preserves spiracles, openings for breathing air, and Kampecaris obanensis comes from the island of Kerrera near Oban. Their ages have been disputed; zircon dating in 2017 placed the Stonehaven beds at about 414 million years, while a 2020 study dated the Kerrera millipede to about 425 million years, making it a candidate for the oldest known land animal. Older trackways in Ordovician and even Cambrian coastal sediments show that arthropods made excursions onto land much earlier, without necessarily living there. The first land communities were dominated by arthropods such as millipedes and early arachnid relatives, living among low plants and feeding on plant debris, fungi and one another.

title: Prototaxites, an enigmatic giant
summary: Trunk-like columns up to about 8 metres tall, Prototaxites towered over Silurian and Devonian landscapes long before true trees.
description: Prototaxites was first described from Devonian rocks of the Gaspé Peninsula, Quebec, by John William Dawson in 1859, who mistook its trunks for decaying conifers. Its trunks, up to about a metre across and perhaps 8 metres tall, were built of interwoven tubes rather than wood, and it was the largest organism on land from the late Silurian into the Devonian, when most plants were less than a metre high. Since the early 2000s it has usually been interpreted as a giant fungus, and carbon-isotope studies indicate that it fed on other organic matter rather than photosynthesising. A 2025 study of specimens from the Rhynie chert argued instead that it belonged to an extinct lineage of complex life distinct from fungi, reviving a long-running debate.
mainstreamView: Most palaeobiologists since about 2001 have classified Prototaxites as a fungus, based on its tubular anatomy and isotopic evidence that it was not photosynthetic, but its exact affinities were never settled. Chemical and anatomical work published in 2025 found a poor match to known fungi, and whether it was a fungus or a member of a now-extinct lineage remains an open question.

title: Rhynie chert
summary: Hot springs at Rhynie, Scotland, petrify an Early Devonian ecosystem cell by cell: plants, fungi, lichens and early arachnids.
description: The Rhynie chert in Aberdeenshire formed when silica-rich water from hot springs flooded a marshy landscape about 407 million years ago, entombing organisms so quickly that individual cells, and even fungi living inside plant tissues, are preserved. It contains early vascular plants such as Rhynia and Aglaophyton, fungi, algae, lichens and arthropods including mites, trigonotarbid arachnids, an early harvestman, springtails and the possible early insect Rhyniognatha. The deposit provides some of the oldest clear evidence of mycorrhiza-like partnerships between plants and fungi, which are thought to have been crucial to the colonisation of land. Discovered by William Mackie in 1912, it remains one of the most important fossil sites for understanding early land ecosystems.

title: Silurian hypothesis (thought experiment)
dateLabel: Hypothetical: any time since complex life spread onto land
summary: A 2018 paper asks whether an industrial civilisation that existed millions of years before humans could still be detected in the rocks.
description: The Silurian hypothesis, named after the reptilian civilisation of the television series Doctor Who rather than directly after the geological period, was posed by climate scientist Gavin Schmidt and astrophysicist Adam Frank in 2018. They asked what geological fingerprint an industrial civilisation would leave and whether it could be recognised after tens or hundreds of millions of years, given that cities and artefacts are unlikely to survive and only a small fraction of the surface is preserved in the rock record. Possible signals include abrupt carbon-isotope shifts, ocean anoxia, unusual sediment and nutrient fluxes, plastics, synthetic compounds and fission products. The authors stated that they strongly doubted any such civilisation had existed; the exercise was meant to sharpen ways of recognising the Anthropocene and possible technosignatures on other planets.
mainstreamView: There is no evidence that any industrial civilisation preceded humans, and the hypothesis's own authors present it as a thought experiment rather than a claim. Known geological anomalies that might superficially resemble an industrial signal, such as the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum or Mesozoic oceanic anoxic events, are explained by natural processes such as volcanism and carbon-cycle feedbacks, unfold over thousands of years rather than centuries, and lack markers such as synthetic molecules or anomalous isotopes. The paper is valued as a framework for detecting human and extraterrestrial technosignatures, not as evidence about Earth's past.

title: Zachełmie trackways
summary: Footprints in a Polish quarry, if made by four-limbed vertebrates, would predate Tiktaalik and its relatives by nearly 20 million years.
description: In 2010 Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and colleagues described trackways from a quarry at Zachełmie in Poland's Holy Cross Mountains, in Middle Devonian sediments about 395 million years old. The prints appear to show digit impressions and an alternating gait, and the authors interpreted them as made by tetrapods up to about 2.5 metres long. If correct, limbed vertebrates existed about 10 million years before the oldest known elpistostegalian body fossils and nearly 20 million years before Tiktaalik, implying a long gap in the fossil record and that Tiktaalik was a late-surviving relative of the first tetrapods rather than an ancestor. The tracks were first thought to have formed on a marine tidal flat, but later work suggested the margins of an ephemeral lake.
mainstreamView: Many researchers accept that at least some of the Zachełmie prints are tetrapod tracks, which would mean the fish-to-tetrapod transition began earlier than body fossils show. Others argue that the marks could have been made by fishes, such as lungfishes feeding or pushing off the bottom, or question how clearly digits are shown. No tetrapod body fossils of this age have been found, so the trackways remain the main evidence for an early origin of limbs.

title: First forests
summary: Fossil trees near Minehead, England, and root systems at Cairo, New York, record the oldest known forests, about 390–386 million years ago.
description: Fossilised trees of the cladoxylopsid Calamophyton in the Hangman Sandstone Formation near Minehead, Somerset, described in 2024 and about 390 million years old, are the oldest known fossil forest. Slightly younger fossil soils in a quarry at Cairo, New York, described in 2019, preserve extensive root systems of the tree Archaeopteris alongside cladoxylopsid trees, and the nearby Gilboa fossil forest preserves stumps of the cladoxylopsid Eospermatopteris. Archaeopteris combined fern-like reproduction by spores with true wood, leafy branches and deep roots, and by the Late Devonian it formed forests worldwide. Trees transformed the planet: deep roots accelerated rock weathering and soil formation, and the burial of plant carbon drew down atmospheric carbon dioxide. Many researchers link these changes to Late Devonian cooling and to nutrient runoff that may have fuelled ocean anoxia during the Late Devonian extinctions, an idea known as the Devonian plant hypothesis.

title: Dunkleosteus and the Devonian 'Age of Fishes'
summary: The armoured placoderm Dunkleosteus, a bony-jawed predator over three metres long, hunts Devonian seas preserved in the Cleveland Shale of Ohio.
description: The Devonian is often called the 'Age of Fishes' because jawed fishes diversified rapidly, from armoured placoderms and spiny acanthodians to early sharks, ray-finned fishes and the lobe-finned fishes that gave rise to tetrapods. Among the largest placoderms was Dunkleosteus, an arthrodire whose head and shoulders were covered in bony armour and whose jaws carried self-sharpening bony blades instead of true teeth; it was one of the first vertebrate apex predators. Its best-known species, D. terrelli, comes from the Late Devonian Cleveland Shale of northern Ohio, where many skulls have been collected since the 19th century. Older estimates of up to 6–10 metres in length have been revised downward, and a 2023 study estimated typical adults at about 3.4 metres and the largest at about 4.1 metres. The placoderms disappeared at the end of the Devonian in the Hangenberg event.

title: Gogo Formation and the oldest known live birth
summary: A fossil reef in Western Australia preserves Devonian fishes in 3-D, including the placoderm Materpiscis with an embryo still attached.
description: The Gogo Formation in the Kimberley region of Western Australia formed around an ancient barrier reef about 380 million years ago, and its limestone nodules preserve fishes in three dimensions, sometimes with muscles, nerves and organs. In 2008 researchers led by John Long described Materpiscis attenboroughi, a small placoderm containing an embryo connected by a mineralised umbilical cord, the oldest known evidence of live birth and internal fertilisation in vertebrates. Other Gogo fossils include the lobe-finned fish Gogonasus, important for understanding the fish-to-tetrapod transition, and, described in 2022, the oldest known three-dimensionally preserved heart of a jawed vertebrate, in an arthrodire placoderm.

title: Tiktaalik, a fish with limb-like fins
summary: On Arctic Canada's Ellesmere Island lies Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck, lungs and sturdy fins bridging fishes and four-limbed animals.
description: Tiktaalik roseae, discovered in 2004 by Neil Shubin, Edward Daeschler and Farish Jenkins in the Fram Formation of Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, was a flat-headed lobe-finned fish up to about 2.7 metres long that lived in shallow streams about 375 million years ago. It combined fish features such as scales, fins and gills with tetrapod-like ones, including a mobile neck, robust ribs, spiracles suggesting air breathing, and pectoral fins containing shoulder, elbow and wrist-like bones that could prop up the body. The team found it by deliberately searching rocks of the right age and environment, a successful prediction of where transitional fossils should occur. Tiktaalik is regarded as a close relative of the ancestors of tetrapods rather than a direct ancestor, especially as the Zachełmie trackways suggest limbed vertebrates may have existed earlier.

title: Late Devonian extinction (Kellwasser event)
summary: Pulses of ocean anoxia at the end of the Frasnian wipe out vast reef systems and much marine life in one of the 'Big Five' extinctions.
description: The Late Devonian extinction was a prolonged crisis rather than a single event, but its most severe phase, the Kellwasser event at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary about 372 million years ago, is named after black shales in the Kellwasser valley of Germany's Harz Mountains. Two pulses of oxygen-poor water swept tropical seas, contributing to the loss of around 70% of marine species by some estimates and devastating the vast stromatoporoid–coral reefs, which did not recover on a similar scale for roughly 100 million years. Trilobites, brachiopods, placoderms and conodonts suffered heavily, while life on land was less affected. Proposed causes include nutrient runoff from the spread of forests, volcanism such as the Viluy Traps in Siberia, climate swings and sea-level changes; an asteroid impact has also been suggested but is not widely supported.

title: Acanthostega and Ichthyostega: limbs with digits
summary: In East Greenland, Acanthostega and Ichthyostega show some of the first true limbs with digits, on animals still living mainly in water.
description: Ichthyostega, collected by Danish expeditions to East Greenland from 1929 and described in 1932, and Acanthostega, named in 1952 from skull fragments and known from complete skeletons collected by Jennifer Clack's team in 1987, lived in the Late Devonian about 365 million years ago. Both had limbs with digits, eight on the forelimb of Acanthostega and seven on the hindlimb of Ichthyostega rather than the five of later tetrapods, but also fish-like tail fins and, in Acanthostega, bones that supported internal gills. Acanthostega's limbs were poorly suited to bearing its weight on land, supporting the idea that digits first evolved for moving through water and vegetation and were only later used for walking. Ichthyostega had a more robust shoulder girdle and may have hauled itself across land somewhat like a seal.

title: Earliest known seeds: Elkinsia in West Virginia
summary: Late Devonian rocks near Elkins, West Virginia, preserve the oldest known seeds, borne in small cups on the fern-like fronds of Elkinsia.
description: The oldest known seeds are the preovules of Elkinsia polymorpha, a seed fern described in 1989 from Late Devonian (Famennian) rocks of the Hampshire Formation near Elkins, West Virginia, about 365 million years old. Each ovule was a spore case partly enclosed by lobed protective tissue and borne in a cup-like cupule at the tip of a fertile frond, while other fronds carried pollen-producing organs. Seeds freed fertilisation from the need for external water and gave the embryo a protected food supply, allowing seed plants eventually to colonise drier habitats. Other seed plants such as Archaeosperma appear in the Famennian, and the seed-like Runcaria from Belgium, about 385 million years old, suggests the lineage began in the Middle Devonian. Seed plants later gave rise to conifers, cycads, ginkgos and, much later, flowering plants.

title: Late Paleozoic icehouse (Karoo ice age)
summary: Ice sheets wax and wane over southern Gondwana for some 100 million years, the longest glaciation of the Phanerozoic.
description: As Gondwana lay across the South Pole and atmospheric carbon dioxide fell, ice sheets formed in several pulses over southern Africa, South America, Antarctica, India and Australia, with the most extensive glaciation in the late Carboniferous and early Permian. Glacial tillite of the Dwyka Group in South Africa's Karoo Basin gives the ice age its alternative name, and matching glacial deposits on now-separated southern continents became key evidence for continental drift. Repeated growth and melting of the ice sheets drove sea-level swings of up to about 100 metres, recorded as cyclothems, rhythmic alternations of marine beds and coal-bearing deposits in the tropics. Carbon burial by the coal forests and weathering of the newly uplifted Central Pangean Mountains are among the proposed causes, and the ice largely disappeared during the Permian.

title: Romer's gap
summary: A puzzling 15-million-year scarcity of tetrapod fossils after the Devonian is being filled by new finds in the Scottish Borders.
description: Romer's gap, named after the palaeontologist Alfred Romer, is an interval at the start of the Carboniferous from which very few tetrapod and fish fossils were long known, separating the aquatic tetrapods of the Devonian from the diverse forms of later Carboniferous. Proposed explanations included low atmospheric oxygen, the aftermath of the end-Devonian extinction, or simply a lack of suitable rocks and collecting effort. Since the 2010s, discoveries at sites such as Burnmouth in the Scottish Borders have yielded many new tetrapods from this interval, suggesting that the gap is largely an artefact of sampling and that tetrapods diversified quickly after the Hangenberg event.

title: Hangenberg event ends the Devonian
summary: A final Devonian crisis of ocean anoxia and brief glaciation ends the armoured placoderm fishes and hits ammonoids and early tetrapods.
description: The Hangenberg event at the end of the Devonian, about 359 million years ago, is marked by a widespread black shale named after a locality in Germany's Sauerland and was accompanied by a brief glaciation in South America and a fall in sea level. It ended the placoderms as a group, nearly wiped out the ammonoids and severely hit early tetrapods and other vertebrates, after which sharks, ray-finned fishes and tetrapods diversified in the Carboniferous. Its causes are debated; proposals include ocean anoxia driven by climate change, volcanism, and a 2020 suggestion that a nearby supernova damaged the ozone layer, based on malformed plant spores of this age.

title: The supercontinent Pangaea
summary: Gondwana collides with Laurussia, welding nearly all land into the supercontinent Pangaea, surrounded by the world ocean Panthalassa.
description: Through the Carboniferous and Permian, the southern supercontinent Gondwana collided with Laurussia in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies, raising the Central Pangean Mountains, whose remnants include the Appalachians, the Mauritanides of West Africa and Europe's Variscan massifs. Siberia and the Kazakh terranes joined later along the Ural Mountains, and by the late Paleozoic most of Earth's land formed a single C-shaped supercontinent stretching nearly from pole to pole, surrounded by Panthalassa with the Paleo-Tethys Ocean in its eastern embayment. The merger mixed previously separate faunas, created vast arid interiors and strongly monsoonal climates, and reduced the area of shallow coastal seas. The name was popularised by Alfred Wegener, whose matching fossils and rock formations across the Atlantic were early evidence for continental drift, and the supercontinent began to break apart about 200 million years ago with the opening of the central Atlantic.

title: Arthropleura, the giant millipede
summary: A fossil from Howick Bay, Northumberland, shows the millipede Arthropleura reached about 2.6 metres, the largest land arthropod known.
description: Arthropleura was a genus of giant millipede-like myriapods that lived in Carboniferous and early Permian forests of Euramerica. A 76-centimetre section of exoskeleton, found in 2018 in a fallen sandstone block at Howick Bay, Northumberland, and described in 2021, indicates an animal about 2.6 metres long and perhaps 50 kilograms, about 326 million years old. Its trackways, up to about half a metre wide, are known from Scotland, Nova Scotia and the United States. Arthropleura's size has often been linked to high atmospheric oxygen, but the Howick specimen predates the late Carboniferous oxygen peak, and its describers suggested that a nutrient-rich diet may also have mattered.

title: Coal forests of the Carboniferous
summary: Swamp forests of giant clubmosses, horsetails and tree ferns cover equatorial Euramerica, burying the carbon that became much of the world's coal.
description: In the late Carboniferous, vast swamp forests grew across the equatorial lowlands of Laurussia, from present-day North America through Britain and Germany to Ukraine. They were dominated by lycopsid trees such as Lepidodendron and Sigillaria, some 30–40 metres tall, together with giant horsetails like Calamites, tree ferns and early seed plants rooted in waterlogged peat. Buried peat became the coal seams of the Ruhr, the Appalachians, South Wales and the Donets Basin that later powered the Industrial Revolution, and gave the period its name, meaning 'coal-bearing'. Why so much plant matter escaped decay is debated: an older idea that fungi had not yet evolved the ability to break down lignin has been challenged by studies attributing the coal mainly to the wet tropical climate and subsiding basins of the time.

title: First amniotes: Hylonomus at Joggins
summary: Small, lizard-like Hylonomus, from fossil tree stumps at Joggins, Nova Scotia, has long been regarded as the oldest known reptile and an early amniote.
description: Amniotes, the group comprising reptiles, birds and mammals, are distinguished by an egg with protective membranes that can develop on dry land, freeing vertebrates from returning to water to breed. Hylonomus lyelli, a lizard-like animal about 20 centimetres long found in the 1850s by John William Dawson inside the hollow stumps of fossil lycopsid trees at Joggins, Nova Scotia, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, has long been regarded as the oldest known reptile, although a 2025 phylogenetic analysis placed it just outside crown-group amniotes. Soon after their origin, amniotes split into the sauropsid line leading to reptiles and birds and the synapsid line leading to mammals. Clawed footprints from Victoria, Australia, described in 2025 and dated to about 355 million years ago, have been interpreted as amniote tracks, which would push the group's origin back by tens of millions of years if confirmed.

title: Carboniferous rainforest collapse
summary: A drier, more seasonal climate breaks up the equatorial coal swamps into isolated refuges, which give way to seed-plant woodlands.
description: Around 305 million years ago, in the Kasimovian age, the lycopsid-dominated coal forests of Euramerica collapsed as the climate became cooler and more seasonally dry, linked to fluctuations of the late Paleozoic ice age and falling carbon dioxide. The swamps broke up into scattered islands of forest, and tree ferns and drought-tolerant seed plants replaced the giant clubmosses in many areas, as recorded in coal mines of the Illinois Basin and elsewhere. A 2010 study argued that this fragmentation reduced amphibian diversity while early reptiles, better suited to drier habitats, diversified, although later analyses have questioned how strongly the plant changes drove tetrapod evolution. Coal swamps persisted in East Asia, where wet forests continued into the Permian.

title: Atmospheric oxygen peaks
summary: Burial of plant carbon pushes atmospheric oxygen probably to its highest level in Earth's history, perhaps 25–35%, compared with 21% today.
description: Geochemical models such as GEOCARBSULF, based on the burial rates of organic carbon and pyrite, suggest that oxygen rose through the Carboniferous to a maximum of perhaps 30–35% of the atmosphere near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, well above today's 21%. The rise is attributed to the burial of enormous quantities of organic carbon in coal swamps and marine sediments, which removed carbon from circulation and left the oxygen released by photosynthesis in the air. High oxygen has been linked to the gigantism of insects and other arthropods and to frequent wildfires, recorded by abundant fossil charcoal. Estimates vary considerably between models and proxies, and some recent reconstructions suggest a lower peak nearer 25–30%.

title: Meganeura and the giant insects
summary: Griffinflies such as Meganeura, with wingspans near 70 centimetres, hunt over the coal swamps of Commentry in central France.
description: Meganeura monyi, described in the 1880s from the late Carboniferous coal measures of Commentry, France, was a dragonfly-like griffinfly (order Meganisoptera) with a wingspan of about 65–70 centimetres, among the largest insects ever. Insects had evolved flight by the mid-Carboniferous, the first animals to do so, and they diversified rapidly in the coal forests alongside cockroach-like insects, mayfly relatives and palaeodictyopterans with sucking beaks. The gigantism of Meganeura and its relatives is commonly attributed to high atmospheric oxygen, which would ease the limits on body size set by insects' tracheal breathing system, although the absence of flying vertebrate predators may also have played a role. Giant griffinflies persisted into the Permian after oxygen levels had begun to fall, which complicates the oxygen explanation.

title: Glossopteris forests spread across Gondwana
summary: Tongue-leaved Glossopteris seed plants dominate southern Gondwana; their fossils are later found from India to Antarctica.
description: As the late Paleozoic ice sheets retreated in the early Permian, forests dominated by Glossopteris, a woody seed plant with tongue-shaped leaves, spread across the cool, wet lowlands of southern Gondwana. Their remains formed major coal deposits in India, South Africa, Australia and Antarctica, and many of the trees probably shed their leaves seasonally to survive dark polar winters. The occurrence of the same flora on continents now separated by oceans, recognised by Eduard Suess in the 19th century, was a central argument of Alfred Wegener and Alexander du Toit for continental drift. Specimens collected near the Beardmore Glacier by Robert Falcon Scott's polar party in 1912, and found with their bodies, helped establish that Antarctica had once supported forests. The Glossopteris flora disappeared in the end-Permian extinction.

title: Dimetrodon and the early synapsids
summary: Sail-backed Dimetrodon, a top predator of early Permian Texas, belongs to the synapsids, the lineage that would eventually produce mammals.
description: Synapsids, identified by a single opening in the skull behind each eye, diverged from the reptile line soon after the origin of amniotes in the late Carboniferous, and in the early Permian they became the dominant large land vertebrates. Dimetrodon, best known from the Red Beds of north-central Texas and named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878, was a predator up to about 3–4 metres long with a tall sail supported by elongated spines on its vertebrae, whose function, whether display, temperature regulation or both, is still debated. Although often mistaken for a dinosaur, it died out roughly 40 million years before the first dinosaurs appeared and is more closely related to mammals than to any reptile. Its name, meaning 'two measures of teeth', refers to the differently shaped teeth along its jaws that foreshadow the specialised teeth of mammals.

title: Mesosaurus links Africa and South America
summary: A small aquatic reptile found only in Brazil, Uruguay and southern Africa becomes classic evidence that the two continents were once joined.
description: Mesosaurus was a slender reptile about a metre long with long jaws and needle-like teeth that lived in a vast, partly enclosed inland sea in southern Gondwana in the early Permian. Its fossils are abundant in the Irati Formation of Brazil, in Uruguay, and in the Whitehill Formation of South Africa and Namibia, but are found nowhere else. Because a small swimmer of shallow waters could not have crossed an ocean, its distribution was cited by Alfred Wegener and Alexander du Toit as evidence that Africa and South America had once been connected. It is among the earliest reptiles known to have returned to life in water, and some specimens preserve embryos, among the oldest known amniote embryos.

title: Olson's extinction
summary: A turnover in Permian land vertebrates, as pelycosaur-grade synapsids give way to therapsids, may or may not have been a mass extinction.
description: Olson's extinction, named after the palaeontologist Everett C. Olson, describes an apparent loss of land vertebrate diversity around the boundary between the early and middle Permian, about 273–270 million years ago. In this interval the pelycosaur-grade synapsids and many amphibians of the Texas Red Beds were replaced by the therapsid-dominated faunas known from Russia's Cis-Urals region around Perm and later from South Africa. The interval coincides with a scarcity of fossil-bearing continental rocks worldwide, sometimes called Olson's gap, which makes the timing and severity of the change hard to measure.
mainstreamView: Whether Olson's extinction was a true mass extinction is unresolved. A 2008 study by Sahney and Benton treated it as a significant drop in diversity, while later analyses that corrected for the sparse rock record found a more gradual, protracted turnover or attributed much of the apparent loss to gaps in sampling and dating. Most researchers agree that a major faunal turnover from pelycosaurs to therapsids occurred, but not on its speed or cause.

title: Therapsids flourish in the Karoo
summary: Mammal-like therapsids such as dinocephalians, dicynodonts and gorgonopsians dominate the Permian Karoo Basin of South Africa.
description: Therapsids, the synapsid group that includes mammals and their extinct relatives, rose to dominance on land in the middle and late Permian, and the Beaufort Group of South Africa's Karoo Basin preserves the most complete record of their evolution. Its rocks contain successive faunas of large herbivorous and carnivorous dinocephalians, tusked plant-eating dicynodonts, sabre-toothed gorgonopsians and small, more mammal-like therocephalians and cynodonts. Therapsids show a progression of mammal-like traits, including more upright limbs, differentiated teeth and, in later forms, a secondary palate that may indicate higher metabolic rates. The Karoo sequence also records the end-Permian extinction on land, which most therapsid groups did not survive, although dicynodonts and cynodonts carried the lineage into the Triassic.

title: Expanding Earth hypothesis
summary: Proponents such as Samuel Warren Carey argued that the continents once covered a much smaller Earth and that oceans opened as it swelled.
description: The expanding Earth hypothesis holds that Earth's radius has grown substantially, so that the continents once fitted together to cover the whole surface of a much smaller planet and today's ocean basins opened as it expanded. An early version was proposed by Ott Christoph Hilgenberg in 1933, and the Australian geologist Samuel Warren Carey of the University of Tasmania, an influential pioneer of continental-drift reconstructions, championed it from the 1950s, arguing that Pangaea could be reassembled without gaps only on a smaller globe. In proponents' reconstructions the late Paleozoic Earth was markedly smaller and lacked deep ocean basins, which formed mostly within the last 200 million years. The idea retains a small following, partly because nearly all existing oceanic crust is younger than about 200 million years.
mainstreamView: Geologists abandoned expanding Earth once plate tectonics showed that new ocean floor created at spreading ridges is balanced by old floor destroyed at subduction zones, which explains why ocean crust is young without any change in Earth's size. Palaeomagnetic studies indicate that Earth's radius in the Paleozoic was within a few percent of today's, and satellite geodesy combining VLBI, laser ranging and GPS has measured any present change in radius at about 0.1 millimetre per year, statistically indistinguishable from zero. No known physical process could add the required mass or lower Earth's density enough, and expanding-Earth reconstructions fail to match the palaeomagnetic latitudes and fossil distributions that plate reconstructions explain.

title: Capitanian extinction and the Emeishan Traps
summary: Eruptions of the Emeishan Traps in south-west China coincide with a severe extinction of tropical marine life at the end of the middle Permian.
description: Near the end of the Capitanian age, the last stage of the middle Permian (Guadalupian), marine life suffered a major extinction that hit large fusulinid foraminifera, reef-building sponges and calcareous algae, brachiopods and bivalves, especially in tropical seas. Its timing closely matches eruptions of the Emeishan large igneous province, whose basalts are exposed at Mount Emei in Sichuan, and volcanic gases are thought to have triggered warming, acidification and loss of oxygen in the oceans. Recognised as a distinct event only since the 1990s, it is now considered by many researchers to be among the larger Phanerozoic extinctions, although its magnitude and whether it was a single global event remain debated.

title: Siberian Traps erupt
summary: Vast eruptions in Siberia pour out millions of cubic kilometres of basalt and bake coal and salt deposits, releasing enormous volumes of gas.
description: The Siberian Traps are among the largest known volcanic provinces, with lava flows and buried intrusions (sills) spread over several million square kilometres around Norilsk and the Tunguska Basin, and estimates of their total volume reach several million cubic kilometres. High-precision uranium–lead dating indicates that the main phase began roughly 300,000 years before the end-Permian extinction and continued for several hundred thousand years afterwards, with a pulse of sill intrusion coinciding with the extinction's onset. Magma intruding sedimentary basins rich in coal, carbonates and evaporites released huge amounts of carbon dioxide, methane and halogen compounds, a mechanism widely regarded as the primary trigger of the extinction through extreme warming, ocean acidification and anoxia. The province also hosts the world's richest nickel–palladium ore deposits at Norilsk.

title: End-Permian mass extinction ('Great Dying')
summary: Earth's worst mass extinction wipes out an estimated 80–90% of marine species and most land vertebrate species in some 60,000 years.
description: The end-Permian extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, was the most severe biotic crisis known: estimates suggest roughly 80–90% of marine species and around 70% of land vertebrate species disappeared, including the last trilobites, the rugose and tabulate corals and most brachiopods, and it is the only mass extinction known to have hit insects heavily. High-precision dating of ash beds at Meishan in Zhejiang, China, where the Permian–Triassic boundary is formally defined, indicates that the main marine extinction took only about 60,000 years. The leading explanation links it to the Siberian Traps: massive releases of carbon dioxide and methane caused rapid warming of tropical seas to perhaps 35–40 °C, ocean acidification and widespread anoxia, with hydrogen sulfide and ozone loss possibly adding to the damage. Recovery took millions of years, and the survivors, including early archosaurs and the ancestors of mammals, set the stage for the Mesozoic.

title: Bedout: an end-Permian impact crater? (fringe)
dateLabel: c. 252 million years ago (as proposed in 2004)
summary: Researchers proposed in 2004 that a buried structure off north-western Australia is a huge impact crater that caused the end-Permian extinction.
description: The Bedout High is a roughly circular structure buried beneath the continental shelf about 250 kilometres off north-western Australia, first suggested as a possible impact site by the geologist John Gorter in 1996. In 2004 Luann Becker and colleagues argued in the journal Science that breccias recovered by the petroleum exploration wells Bedout-1 and Lagrange-1 were impact melt rocks showing shock metamorphism, dated them to about 250 million years ago, and proposed that the structure is the core of a crater roughly 200 kilometres across formed at the time of the end-Permian extinction. The same group had earlier reported fullerene molecules carrying extraterrestrial noble gases from Permian–Triassic boundary layers as further evidence of an impact. The idea attracted wide attention because an asteroid impact had already been shown to explain the end-Cretaceous extinction.
mainstreamView: Most geologists reject Bedout as an impact crater and as the cause of the end-Permian extinction. Re-examination of the well samples identified altered volcanic rocks rather than impact melt, convincing shocked minerals have not been confirmed, and the structure is more simply explained by rifting and volcanism along the continental margin. An impact of the proposed size would have spread an ejecta layer around the world, but boundary sections such as Meishan show no ejecta layer or iridium anomaly comparable to that of the end-Cretaceous impact, and the fullerene noble-gas results could not be reproduced by other laboratories. High-precision dating instead ties the extinction closely to the Siberian Traps eruptions, which are widely accepted as its main trigger.
